patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2014: Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission national inquiry into bacha bazi (2014).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role_note: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017 (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017; Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified); Bacha bazi — boys abused by Afghan commanders; US forces told not to intervene; Afghanistan — Human Rights Commission national inquiry into bacha bazi (2014); Afghanistan — students report sexual abuse in Taliban-run madrasahs.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified)
cases.who: Taliban de facto authorities
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 12 children (6 boys, 6 girls) in Afghanistan in 2023, 10 attributed to the Taliban, and the abduction of 3 children by the Taliban for sexual violence purposes. It verified 13 cases in 2022 (Taliban 7) and 6 in 2024 (Taliban 5).

cases.title: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
cases.who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
cases.what: In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore sexual abuse of boys by Afghan allies, describing it as rampant; nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) to investigate. SIGAR's report, sent to Congress in 2017 and made public on 23 January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and said 'the full extent of child sexual assault committed by Afghan security forces may never be known'. The Pentagon used the 'notwithstanding' exception to the Leahy Law to keep supporting implicated units, including approving continued funding in December 2015 for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.
cases.cover_up: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).

cases.title: Afghanistan — Human Rights Commission national inquiry into bacha bazi (2014)
cases.who: Powerful men who keep boys for dancing and sexual abuse
cases.what: The Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission concluded a national inquiry into the causes and consequences of bacha bazi, the sexual abuse of boys kept by powerful men to dance, in August 2014. It held 71 focus groups and 17 public hearings in 17 provinces, attended by almost 2,200 people, and two-thirds of victims said they received money from the perpetrators. Its chair, Sima Samar, said the practice was a crime that the law did not properly prevent and called on the government to fight the culture of impunity.
cases.cover_up: The Commission's chair said the law did not properly prevent the practice and called for an end to the 'culture of impunity'

cases.title: Afghanistan — students report sexual abuse in Taliban-run madrasahs
cases.who: Taliban-run madrasah system (6,836 male madrasahs per a Feb 2024 UN report)
cases.what: In March 2024 RFE/RL's Radio Azadi published accounts from male students aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs in western and southwestern Afghanistan who said teachers pressured them and classmates into sexual acts and used corporal punishment; some left school. The report cited a February 2024 UN report counting 6,836 Taliban-established madrasahs for boys and a decree seeking 100,000 new madrasah teachers.
cases.cover_up: A 16-year-old said he reported a teacher to the school's qari, who only told the teacher to stop; the teacher admitted it and continued. The schools are run by the de facto Taliban authorities.

cases.title: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
cases.who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
cases.what: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 5,456 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 2000: Brazil: 2000 law punishing subjecting a child or adolescent to prostitution with 4-10 years
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

cases.title: Brazil — three Arapiraca priests convicted (Penedo diocese)
cases.who: Diocese of Penedo
cases.what: On 19 December 2011 a juvenile court judge in Arapiraca convicted Monsignor Luiz Marques Barbosa (21 years), Monsignor Raimundo Gomes and Fr Edílson Duarte (16 years 4 months each) of abusing altar boys. The case began with complaints from former altar boys in March 2010 and a secretly filmed video broadcast on SBT television.
cases.cover_up: According to the victims, Bishop Valério Breda knew what was happening; he suspended the priests two days after the scandal broke. The convicted priests were not jailed pending appeal.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Brazil — Joint Congressional Inquiry (CPMI) into networks sexually exploiting children (2004)
cases.who: Networks including politicians, businessmen and clergy named by the commission
cases.what: A joint commission of 11 senators and 11 deputies, created in 2003 to investigate violence and networks of sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, had by May 2004 received more than 800 complaints, heard more than 300 people and visited 14 states. Its final report, approved on 13 July 2004, put more than 250 people on notice, among them 20 serving politicians (including one federal deputy, two state deputies and three mayors), about 30 businessmen and five priests, and passed the cases to federal and state prosecutors. The commission's bill rewriting the Penal Code chapter on 'crimes against public morals' (PLS 253/2004) became Law 12.015 of 2009.

cases.title: Brazil — Senate 'CPI da Pedofilia' on online abuse material and child abuse (2008–2010)
cases.who: Users of the Orkut social network and offenders across Brazil; the CPI's hearings were credited with the fall of a Pará state deputy, Luiz Afonso Sefer, convicted at first instance in 2010
cases.what: The Federal Senate's parliamentary inquiry into paedophilia, chaired by Senator Magno Malta, worked for almost three years, the longest CPI to date, and its rapporteur Demóstenes Torres handed a final report of nearly 1,700 pages to police and prosecutors in December 2010. It signed a conduct agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to lift secrecy on Orkut pages linked to child sexual abuse. Rádio Senado reported that hundreds of people were arrested or indicted after its work, and Malta credited the CPI's hearings with the fall of Belém state deputy Luiz Afonso Sefer; Sefer was convicted in 2010 of raping a child, but the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal and, as of February 2026, his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. Laws passed during its work criminalised possession of child abuse material and ordered the closure of businesses where children were exploited.

cases.title: Brazil — Chamber of Deputies inquiry asks indictment of 37, including a mayor and state deputies (2014)
cases.who: Local politicians and others in Amazonas, Minas Gerais and other states
cases.what: A parliamentary inquiry of the Chamber of Deputies, installed in 2012 with Deputy Liliam Sá as rapporteur, approved its final report on 4 June 2014. It asked for the indictment of 37 people for sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, among them the mayor of Coari (Amazonas), Adail Pinheiro, a serving Amazonas state deputy, a former state deputy and a former president of the Três Corações city council.

cases.title: Brazil — Federal Highway Police 'Projeto Mapear' of child sexual exploitation points on highways
cases.who: Truck stops, bars, motels along federal highways
cases.what: Brazil's Federal Highway Police (PRF) and Childhood Brasil have mapped roadside sites vulnerable to child sexual exploitation for about 19 years. The 2021–2022 survey, released 31 May 2023, assessed more than 9,700 points, rating 640 critical and about 1,800 high-risk; the worst conditions were on BR-116 (12 critical points), BR-153, BR-101, BR-163, BR-232 and BR-040. An earlier edition found 69% of victims female and 22% transgender, and 38% from elsewhere, possibly trafficked. The 2025 US TIP report says child sex trafficking is common along BR-386, BR-116 and BR-255.

cases.title: Operation Lobos / Baby Heart (Brazil-led)
cases.who: Baby Heart and other Tor boards
cases.what: A year-long global investigation into the Tor child-abuse site 'Babyheart' and its administrator involved the UK NCA and West Midlands Police, Australian Federal Police and Queensland's Task Force Argos, Toronto Police, the Brazilian Federal Police, INTERPOL, Europol and US ICE, with nine countries listed (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Portugal, the US and the UK). Intelligence narrowed the administrator's location to Portugal, where the Portuguese Judicial Police arrested and charged him in 2017; examination of his devices identified seven victims directly related to him. INTERPOL and Portuguese police presented the case publicly on 23 January 2020. Brazil's Federal Police ran related 'Operação Lobos' phases.

cases.title: Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreaming (2026)
cases.who: Discord Inc.
cases.what: On 12 August 2026 Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) ordered Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature nationwide, saying it had found 'robust evidence' that Discord failed to take reasonable steps to stop minors being exposed to content promoting violence, self-harm and suicide. The order followed the death in July 2026 of a 13-year-old girl in central-western Brazil who, authorities said, was encouraged during a Discord livestream to take her own life. Five teenagers were arrested in connection with her death, and police said the investigation also led them to another girl at risk, whom they reached in time. A Justice Ministry cyber-intelligence official called the case 'a terrible failure in moderation'.

cases.title: Brazil — child sex tourism in northeastern coastal cities (Fortaleza, Natal, Recife, Salvador)
cases.who: Taxi drivers, hotel and bar staff facilitating foreign offenders
cases.what: In 2006 Brazil's Federal Police described sex tourism as most frequent in Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador and Natal, and ran periodic raids, e.g. on a Ponta Negra (Natal) nightclub with 110 foreigners (no children found that night). The 2025 US TIP report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in coastal tourist destinations facilitate child sex trafficking, and cites a study suggesting up to 16 per cent of girls aged 14–17 in one northeastern metropolitan area were likely victims of commercial sexual exploitation.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: no investigations of complicit officials reported; a 2016 child sex-trafficking case involving an elected official in Paraná unresolved.

flows.what: New Tribes Mission missionary Warren Scott Kennell abused Katukina girls while posted in Brazil; he was arrested on return at Orlando airport and jailed for 58 years in 2014. Brazil endpoint is a country centroid.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: New Tribes Mission (Ethnos360)
networks.what: Evangelical mission to indigenous peoples. Abuse documented at its Fanda school in Senegal (GRACE 2010) and by a missionary convicted for abusing Katukina girls in Brazil (2014).

patterns.role_note: 33,303 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2007: suspension: Ireland's Adoption Board suspends adoptions from Ethiopia and Rwanda (10 October) 2009: suspension: Dutch agency Wereldkinderen halts Ethiopian adoptions (23 September); Australia suspends all adoptions from Ethiopia (28 December) 2011: licence revoked: Better Futures Adoption Services loses Ethiopian licence after US finds involvement in child trafficking (February) 2016: suspension: Denmark stops all adoptions from Ethiopia (March) after inspections 2017: suspension: Ethiopia suspends foreign adoptions (November; pending cases continue) 2018: ban: Ethiopia bans adoption by foreigners (January; law effective 18 February 2018)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role_note: Ethiopia — Tigray war sexual violence including girls (ICHREE; UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Ethiopia — Tigray war sexual violence including girls (ICHREE; UN verified); Ethiopia — girls trafficked to Djibouti, Sudan and Saudi Arabia (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Ethiopia — Tigray war sexual violence including girls (ICHREE; UN verified)
cases.who: Ethiopian National Defence Forces, Eritrean Defence Forces, Amhara forces and Tigrayan forces
cases.what: The International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (October 2022) documented Tigrayan forces' rapes of women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages such as Chenna in 2021, alongside widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray. BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at Mekelle health facilities as rape survivors. The UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia in 2024, 38 attributed to the ENDF.

cases.title: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
cases.who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
cases.what: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Ethiopia — girls trafficked to Djibouti, Sudan and Saudi Arabia (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers and begging rings
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Ethiopian women and children in forced begging, sometimes via organized begging rings, in Saudi Arabia, and exploit Ethiopian girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs for control. Reports of official complicity continued.

networks.name: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM)
networks.what: AU peace operation in Somalia. HRW in 2014 documented rape and sexual exploitation of women and girls as young as 12 on Mogadishu bases by Ugandan and Burundian soldiers.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2002: UNHCR–Save the Children UK report and OIOS investigation, West Africa 'sex for aid' (2002).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
cases.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
cases.what: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

cases.title: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea
cases.who: Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA)
cases.what: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. After 30 alumni asked for an investigation in 1995, an independent commission of inquiry heard 80 testimonies and reported in April 1998 that the denomination had been negligent; it identified nine offenders, and abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The US C&MA board issued an open letter asking victims' forgiveness.
cases.cover_up: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2003: Hong Kong: Prevention of Child Pornography Ordinance (Dec 2003) gives extraterritorial effect to 24 sexual offences
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in Hong Kong (IWF 2023–2024)
flows.what: Hong Kong was the third/fourth largest host in 2023–2024 before falling sharply in 2025.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Johnny Kitagawa: first report 1999, first action 2023 (24 years). Shūkan Bunshun's 1999 series; Kitagawa won a defamation judgment (2002) but courts upheld the abuse reporting (2003-04); Japanese mainstream media barely covered it
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: 2023: June 2023 Penal Code reform extended limitation for rape from 10 to 15 years and raised age of consent from 13 to 16; survivor group Spring said it was not enough
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

cases.title: Okinawa — rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen (1995)
cases.who: US Navy and Marine Corps personnel from Camp Hansen
cases.what: In September 1995 three US servicemen based on Okinawa abducted and raped a 12-year-old Okinawan schoolgirl. They were tried in a Japanese court and in 1996 were each found guilty and sentenced to between six years and six months and seven years in prison. The case triggered mass protests against the US bases.

cases.title: Japan — Bishops' Conference survey: 16 cases
cases.who: Catholic Bishops' Conference of Japan (16 dioceses)
cases.what: The Catholic Bishops' Conference of Japan began a survey of all 16 dioceses in May 2019 and published it on 7 April 2020. It found 16 cases of sexual abuse of minors from the 1950s to the 2010s, called 'the tip of the iceberg'. Most victims took 10 to 30 years to report, some 50 to 70 years. Of the accused, seven were Japanese priests and eight religious or missionaries, seven of them foreign. Earlier internal surveys (2002, 2012) had found two and five cases.
cases.cover_up: Eight accused clerics were transferred; some punished clerics kept working or moved to another diocese; five remained priests. Only one denied case was examined by a third-party panel.

cases.title: Johnny Kitagawa — Johnny & Associates talent agency
cases.who: Johnny Kitagawa (founder, Johnny & Associates; now Smile-Up)
cases.what: An external investigation set up by Johnny & Associates concluded on 29 Aug 2023 that founder Johnny Kitagawa had sexually abused minors aspiring to be pop singers for decades; the BBC summarises the finding as abuse of hundreds of boys and young men over a six-decade career. The company admitted the abuse in September 2023, split into a new talent agency (Starto Entertainment) and Smile-Up, which handles compensation through a relief committee of three former judges. The BBC documentary 'Predator' (March 2023) and a former trainee's public allegations in April 2023 triggered the reckoning. In March 2024 Smile-Up's CEO told the BBC he believed two more perpetrators had worked at the agency. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.
cases.cover_up: Media silence: Shukan Bunshun's 2001 reports were upheld on the sexual allegations by the courts (damages reduced 2003; Supreme Court rejected appeal 2004), yet Japanese media barely covered them; journalists attributed this to the agency's power over talent bookings. Earliest cited report: Weekly Sankei, 1965.

cases.title: Japan — Yomiuri survey of sexual misconduct by staff in children's homes
cases.who: Children's homes (児童養護施設) in Japan
cases.what: A Yomiuri Shimbun survey published in December 2021 found that in the five years to fiscal 2020 at least 47 staff at children's homes across Japan were confirmed to have committed indecent acts against children in their care, and that 69 children were victims. Only a summary of the survey was accessible; the full article was withdrawn by the provider.

cases.title: Japan — 'JK business' and compensated dating (police survey 2024; US TIP 2025)
cases.who: JK businesses, often with organized-crime ties
cases.what: The 'JK business' sells simulated dates and services with high-school girls. A National Police Agency survey at the end of December 2024 counted 91 establishments advertising in this way, 70 per cent in Tokyo. Kanagawa first regulated it in 2011 and Tokyo enacted a dedicated ordinance in 2017. The 2025 US TIP report says JK variants and 'compensated dating', often tied to organized crime, continue to facilitate sex trafficking of Japanese children and of children from China, South Korea, Laos, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam.

networks.name: Johnny & Associates (now Smile-Up)
networks.what: Japan's dominant boy-band talent agency. Its founder Johnny Kitagawa abused boys and young men from the early 1970s to the mid-2010s (independent investigation, 2023); the company admitted it and by Aug 2026 had decided to compensate 585 people.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
cases.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
cases.what: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
cases.cover_up: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action

cases.title: Liberia — post-war orphanage boom and adoption fraud
cases.who: Private orphanages and adoption facilitators
cases.what: After the civil war ended in 2003 the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 'orphans' returned to their families. A 2007 UNICEF/Holt International report found many children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN Mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.

cases.title: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
cases.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
cases.what: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

flows.title: Monrovia → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Monrovia, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 353 in FY2006).

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2015: Moss Review into allegations at the Nauru Regional Processing Centre.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Nauru detention centre — Moss Review and Senate inquiry on abuse of asylum-seeker children (2015).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Nauru detention centre — Moss Review and Senate inquiry on abuse of asylum-seeker children (2015)
cases.who: Australian-funded Regional Processing Centre on Nauru; contracted guards and staff
cases.what: The Moss Review, commissioned by the Australian government and published in March 2015, was aware of three rape allegations at the Australian-run Regional Processing Centre on Nauru, one involving a minor, confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child, and concluded that guards trading marijuana with detainees for sexual favours was possibly occurring. In April 2015 staff alleged multiple instances of sexual abuse of women and children in an open letter. A Senate select committee reported on 31 August 2015 in 'Taking responsibility: conditions and circumstances at Australia's Regional Processing Centre in Nauru'.
cases.cover_up: Staff wrote in an open letter in April 2015 that the Australian government had known of alleged abuses against women and children for more than 18 months

cases.title: Australia — 'The Forgotten Children': national inquiry into children in immigration detention
cases.who: Australian Government immigration detention (onshore centres and Nauru regional processing centre)
cases.what: The Australian Human Rights Commission's national inquiry, 'The Forgotten Children', was tabled in Federal Parliament on 11 February 2015. It reported 33 incidents of reported sexual assault in immigration detention between January 2013 and March 2014, 'the vast majority involving children'. A separate government-commissioned review by Philip Moss (March 2015) on the Nauru centre was aware of three rape allegations, one involving a minor, and confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Dominican Republic → Poland: Fr Wojciech Gil.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Fr Wojciech Gil (accused with Wesołowski) (2013): Arrested in Poland 17 Feb 2014; convicted in Poland (seven years, per NCR citation)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 5,036 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Poland — State Commission on Paedophilia, first and second reports (2021–2022)
cases.who: Polish justice system; Catholic clergy (almost 30% of perpetrators in the cases studied)
cases.what: Poland's State Commission on Paedophilia, set up by the government after a 2020 documentary on abuse and alleged cover-ups in the Catholic Church, published its first report on 29 July 2021. It analysed 345 cases and 245 court proceedings involving 188 girls and 173 boys, most aged 11 to 15. Almost 30% of perpetrators were clergy and 35% were relatives. In half the cases no one had noticed signs of abuse. The commission sent 137 notifications to prosecutors and made 22 recommendations, including ending the statute of limitations for child sexual abuse. Its second report, published on 2 August 2022, covered 513 cases; among abusers who were not relatives, clergy were the largest professional group (57 cases, about 47%).

cases.title: Poland — Diocese of Sosnowiec independent commission (2026)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Sosnowiec
cases.what: The independent commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', set up in October 2024 and chaired by journalist Tomasz Krzyżak, presented its findings on 12 February 2026 after reviewing diocesan files from 1992 to January 2025. It found at least 50 children harmed, 96% of them under 15, and 29 people accused, 23 of them diocesan clergy; 19 of the 23 priests were confirmed offenders in church or state proceedings. Bishops were repeatedly alerted but in some cases took no action, and accused priests were often transferred rather than punished. The commission reported eight people to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Bishops were repeatedly alerted, including by reliable sources, but often took no action; where they acted, they usually moved the priest to another parish.

cases.title: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops
cases.who: Polish Episcopal Conference; Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź; Bishop Edward Janiak; Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz
cases.what: In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference released a study reporting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and 'Hide and Seek' (May 2020) led to Vatican investigations of bishops under Vos estis lux mundi. In June 2020 Pope Francis put the Diocese of Kalisz under an apostolic administrator and on 17 October 2020 accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused in 'Hide and Seek' of failing to act against an accused priest. Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was also investigated, and on 6 November 2020 the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz, who died ten days later.
cases.cover_up: Bishops sanctioned by the Vatican for protecting abusers: Janiak (Kalisz) ordered to resign June 2020; Głódź (Gdańsk) removed August 2020 after covering up abuse by Henryk Jankowski and Franciszek Cybula

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
cases.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cases.what: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
cases.cover_up: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.

cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
cases.cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic

flows.what: Suspended in May 2013, Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic; Polish police arrested him in 2014 using Dominican evidence and he was jailed for seven years in 2015.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

cases.who: Russian armed forces and authorities

cases.title: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
cases.who: Telegram (messaging platform)
cases.what: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram was not a member of NCMEC or the IWF and had ignored repeated requests to join. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

cases.title: Blue Orchid — Russian site selling abuse videos
cases.who: Blue Orchid website
cases.what: A Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. The investigation began in May 2000 when Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help; Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By 26 March 2001 US Customs announced that four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, with customers arrested in California, New York and Indiana and leads passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers lure girls and women from rural Kazakhstan and neighbouring Central Asian, East Asian and Eastern European countries with job offers as waitresses, models or nannies in large cities, and exploit Kazakh women and girls in Russia, Uzbekistan, the Middle East, Europe, East Asia and the US.
